title: Canada holds at 2.25% as slack offsets the cost of adjusting to US tariffs
summary: The Bank of Canada left its overnight rate target at 2.25% on 28 January, alongside a Bank Rate of 2.5% and a deposit rate of 2.20%. Governing Council judged the existing stance appropriate if the economy followed the January projection. The growth and inflation outlook had changed little from October, even as uncertainty about US policy and geopolitical developments increased. This distinction between the central projection and the range of outcomes explains how a hold could coexist with an explicit willingness to respond. The decision announcement identifies no timing or direction for the next move and supplies no market-implied rate path against which to measure a surprise (opening and policy paragraphs).

The domestic activity data pulled in different directions. Output had been strong in the third quarter but the Bank thought GDP probably stalled in the fourth. That last assessment was a contemporaneous estimate. US tariffs continued to disrupt exports, while domestic demand appeared to be strengthening. Recent employment gains sat alongside 6.8% unemployment and few businesses reporting plans to add workers. Those details qualify a reading of the previous quarter's growth as evidence of sustained momentum. A slower-growing population and the time needed to adapt to US protectionism also limited near-term growth. The release offers no numerical estimate of how much of the weakness represented lost productive capacity.

The projection rested on consumption holding up, business investment gradually recovering and fiscal policy offering support. The Bank expected Canadian output to grow 1.1% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. These are annual forecasts, distinct from the estimate for the preceding quarter. One particularly important contingency was the forthcoming review of the Canada–US–Mexico Agreement. The release identifies the review as a source of uncertainty without specifying its outcome or assigning it a probability. The policy implication is conditional. If the assumptions underpinning domestic demand or trade changed, the rationale for the prevailing rate would need to be reassessed.

December's rise in headline inflation to 2.4% did not overturn the inflation outlook. The Bank attributed part of the rise to the comparison with the previous winter's GST/HST holiday. Inflation excluding tax changes had been slowing since September, and preferred measures of core inflation had eased from 3% in October to around 2.5% in December. The 2.1% inflation figure refers to 2025 as a whole. Looking forward, the Bank expected inflation close to 2% as trade-related costs and excess supply exerted opposing influences. A weaker export economy could therefore coexist with upward pressure on some prices. An investor assessing the next decision would need evidence about both channels.

The external assumptions provide another check on the forecast. US growth had exceeded expectations, helped by AI investment and household spending. Tariffs were supporting US inflation, with the effect expected to fade gradually later in 2026. Euro-area services were providing support and fiscal policy was expected to add to it. In China, weaker domestic demand was expected to outweigh some export strength. The Bank projected average global growth of about 3% over its forecast horizon. Financial conditions remained generally accommodative. US dollar weakness had lifted the Canadian dollar above US$0.72, broadly in the range seen since October, and the oil-price assumption was slightly lower than in the October report despite geopolitical volatility. These were inputs into the outlook. The announcement presents neither an exchange-rate objective nor an oil-price recommendation. The next scheduled decision was 18 March, with the next Monetary Policy Report due on 29 April (international outlook and information note).

questions.question: Which evidence would show that weaker demand is overwhelming the price effects of trade adjustment?
questions.detail: The Bank expects the two forces broadly to offset. It quantifies neither the size of the output gap nor the pass-through from tariffs. Compare the January Monetary Policy Report's assumptions with subsequently available tax-adjusted CPI components, business selling-price intentions and capacity-use measures. A broad softening in prices alongside greater slack would carry different implications for short Canadian rates from a decline concentrated in a few goods.

questions.question: Can domestic spending sustain the projected recovery in GDP?
questions.detail: The release describes an apparent recovery in demand while fourth-quarter GDP likely stalled and hiring intentions remained subdued. The composition of spending and the contribution from inventory swings are unresolved here. Reconcile household consumption, private fixed investment and trade in the expenditure accounts, then compare them with survey intentions and fiscal implementation. The answer matters to the durability of the projected acceleration from 2026 into 2027.

questions.question: Where would a change in US trade policy first become visible?
questions.detail: The agreement review is an important uncertainty, but the announcement does not identify a specific outcome embedded in market prices. Examine the MPR's policy assumptions and compare customs data, export orders and capital spending intentions across more and less exposed industries. A deterioration in orders before a material change in tariffs would give investors a different timing signal from immediate price pass-through after a formal policy change.
